blogs.author: Jack Clark
blogs.description: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to…
blogs.content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

 Subscribe now

 Here’s a speech I gave on Saturday the 17th of October at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. While we all may quibble over the details, I think it’s evident we’re in the early stages of the singularity, and I wanted to use my privileged position of giving the Per Jacobsson lecture to try and tell the assembled audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers, that they should expect significant, rapid change in the future. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues.

 As I said a few times in the speech – some of which was ad libbed and not captured here – I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. I find myself both a narrator of what is happening in AI, a principle agent behind what is happening in AI, and a translator that goes between many communities. In all of this, I am seeking to be truthful and to be clear about my own culpability. This is a forever work-in-progress.

 Thank you all for reading. Speeches like this draw heavily from the newsletter, and the newsletter is my attempt to provide week-by-week information to all of you. I appreciate your readership.

 ***
 Inside the Event Horizon: Why Everyone Should Take AI Progress Seriously

 Hello, thank you for having me. It is a great privilege to be here.

 To start, I should list my relevant credentials: I am a human being. There is one of me. It has taken me almost 40 years to build the experience to give this speech. I will come back to those credentials later.

 My whole career has been defined by finding information that seemed important to the future of the world, then telling the world about that information.Two decades ago, I started my career as a journalist, focusing on data centers. Through that work, I became so obsessed with AI that in 2016 I left journalism to work at OpenAI, then co-founded Anthropic a few years later. Ever since, I’ve been trying to convince the world that one day, AI systems might become so powerful that they could alter national security, change the economic trajectory of the planet, and perhaps eventually gain the ability to build themselves.

 Well, the moment has arrived. AI is now changing national security, it is altering the economic trajectory of the world – as we’ve heard in so many sessions here – and is contributing to its own development.

 Of course, many of you know this, and you are having to track AI as one of a multitude of destabilizing forces that is shaping your world and your work.

 What I am here to explain today is that AI is on a course to bring about even more change than what we are expecting and we should prepare accordingly. And I’m going to explain why.

 For many years, researchers and science fiction authors have forecast a future in which AI systems drastically increase the pace of overall scientific and technical progress, making things move so quickly that it is hard for humans to keep up.

 They call this the singularity. I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun.

 The writer Vernor Vinge forecast this in 1993. “When greater-than-human intelligence drives progress, that progress will be much more rapid. In fact, there seems no reason why progress itself would not involve the creation of still more intelligent entities — on a still-shorter time scale,” he wrote, describing the singularity as “a point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules.”

 The singularity is here . The implications reach across every aspect of life. But the most important implication is a simple one: we should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI, but science as a whole, will speed up. This will feel confusing and disorienting, and it will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril.

 Today, I’m going to concentrate on the first point: the potential benefits of rapid AI progress, and what we need to do to share in these benefits together.

 So many of the ways that humanity will benefit from AI come from science. I believe that AI-driven scientific invention will change the course of the global economy, alter the ways countries plan and build their own infrastructure, make us all healthier and able to spend more time with our loved ones, and –– at the same time –– cause us all to ask deep philosophical questions about choices we should make about its continued development.

 I’ll develop my claim: For the last half century, most countries have dealt with falling research productivity while researcher headcount grows rapidly – ideas and inventions appear to be getting harder to find.

 But something important has changed: we’ve now built AI systems which have been able to augment, extend, and automate aspects of human labor. This has most obviously happened in software development, where AI systems are now more capable and efficient than the vast majority of the world’s software engineers.

 As a consequence, the field of software development is changing – A single person is now able to write software for anything they can imagine, creating things that previously would have taken entire teams of humans.

 We’ve seen concrete evidence of this inside Anthropic, where our researchers now produce almost 10 times the amount of code than they did for the first four years of the company’s life.

 But new AI capabilities bring new challenges – the coding improvements have meant AI systems have got much better at cybersecurity and cyberattacks –– leading the world to race to deploy these powerful capabilities to create better cyberdefenses, while bad actors race to use these systems to carry out hacks.

 The important thing to notice here is that these things are bound up, inseparably – the advance of AI systems in a general area like coding has also created both positive and negative impacts in domains of international relevance, like cybersecurity.

 This is a taste of things to come. Of progress yielding new capabilities, and new challenges.

 These capabilities will not stop at coding; the same thing will happen to science and robotics. It has already begun to happen. And it means some important properties of the global economy may change – like the rate of innovation, or the frequency with which we invent entirely new general purpose technologies that create new industries around themselves, like the internet, phones, and artificial intelligence.

 So, what causes me to believe this? In 2026, we have got the first signs that AI systems may be capable of doing science at the frontier, and we have some evocative examples of what the future could look like. For instance:

 In mathematics, AI systems have been used to propose solutions to longstanding mathematical problems, like the Navier Stokes Millenium Prize, the Jacobian Conjecture, and several open Erdos problems. In many cases, AI systems were responsible for core insights that made the solution possible.

 In biology, researchers have used AI to design viruses from scratch, to identify new drug candidates for testing, and there are already drugs in trials today which have been in large part designed by AI.

 In robotics, AI systems are now increasingly able to autonomously operate laboratory equipment remotely, making it possible for us to further automate experimentation in domains from biology to materials science, making progress faster in areas like batteries and fuel-cell development.

 Taken individually, each of these examples is exciting. But the profound fact is that they all relate to the same underlying technology – and for most of these use-cases, the same single underlying frontier model. We now have singular entities – AI systems like Claude or ChatGPT or Gemini – which can carry out work at the frontier of multiple scientific disciplines.

 Quantitative metrics bear this out.
 One such metric is the score of AI systems at a test called Humanity’s Last Exam – I didn’t choose the name!

 This ominously named test was developed in response to the profound advances seen in prior years by AI systems at a variety of difficult and varied scientific challenges, covering topics as varied as advanced chemistry, computer science, mathematics, classical literature, and ecology.

 When the exam launched in January 2025, top scoring AI systems obtained a score of 8%. As of this week, the highest scoring system is Claude Opus 5.5 with 67.7%.

 Another example is FrontierMath, a test released in November 2024 that sought to assess how well AI systems could solve hundreds of challenging math problems, curated and evaluated by professional mathematicians. When it launched, the best scoring systems got 2%. Now, they get 94%.

 More broadly, it looks like this everywhere. Pick your favorite part of science and go looking for a test and you’ll find this pattern – sudden and steep increases in capability, everywhere you look.

 TheoPhysEval
I’ll close my evidence with a story. The latest example comes to us from a paper published just last week, called TheoPhysEval. This is a paper that tests out how well AI systems can solve unpublished problems in theoretical physics. The 50 questions in the paper were compiled by physicists around the world.

 Unsurprisingly, AI systems got high scores. But what is surprising is how they got the high scores. Here, I am going to quote from Indian physicist Suvrat Raju, who wrote a post commenting on the results .

 “I don’t know of any individual who can solve any significant fraction of our final collection of problems without AI assistance,” he said. “Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5. But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50).”

 Think about this for a moment. Some of the world’s scientific experts built a test out of problems an AI could never have possibly read the answer to. And when they tested the AI, not only did it score high, but it got a higher score by finding errors in the answers that the humans had worked on!

 There is a scene in films, usually two thirds of the way through, when the young protagonist finally proves to their mentor that they have what it takes to go out into the world and succeed independently. It is a narrative trope – when the teacher becomes the student. That is what is happening here.

 So, why am I telling you this? Why does it matter that AI systems are getting better at science?

 I believe it is because doing true frontier science – being capable of making breakthroughs that extend the frontier of knowledge – implicitly tests for one of the last frontiers of AI capability: creativity. My view is that if AI systems can creatively problem solve to succeed at science, we should expect this to be a sign of their ability to generalize into many domains, including certainly AI research itself, which could have an explosive effect on innovation.

 Therefore, if AI systems get better at science, this will strongly drive the growth and shape of the future economy, which means that you can make decisions today to set up...

blogs.title: Do You Trust Apple?
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description:
Listen to this post: Log in to listen

On July 21, 1999, Steve Jobs did something remarkable at Macworld…
blogs.content:
Listen to this post :

 Log in to listen

 On July 21, 1999, Steve Jobs did something remarkable at Macworld New York: first he went to Apple.com, then to “CNN Interactive”, then to Disney.com. That wasn’t the remarkable part: what blew the crowd away was when he picked up the just-introduced iBook and walked around while waiting for Disney.com to load. The crowd went wild at the lack of wires:

 I’m not going to quote this entire product introduction, but I’ve clipped the whole thing for your enjoyment; here are a few pertinent parts of Jobs’ introduction of what he called “AirPort”, and what the rest of the industry called “WiFi”:

 There is one more thing.

 The main point of this keynote was the aforementioned introduction of the original iBook:

 This meant that “one more thing” was in fact not just an extra unexpected product, but an explicit addition to the primary product’s feature set.

 No wire. What is going on here? We are really excited to announce, in addition to iBook, AirPort wireless networking…It’s a wireless LAN. It runs at 11 megabits per second, and it’s based on industry standards. This is 802.11 wireless networking, and everybody is jumping on board with this thing over the next six to nine months. So all sorts of devices are going to be able to interact with AirPorts. We’re just going to be there first and best, and the specification also incorporates quite a bit of privacy protection, so everything you send out is encrypted. A lot of privacy. We’ve worked with Lucent on this for the last 18 months, hand-in-hand to marry their wireless technology with our ease-of-use technology and to bring the cost of this down for people, because this stuff has been pretty pricey to date.

 Apple’s selling proposition has, in many respects, never changed: modern technology that is easy to use and private too.

 So AirPort, what is it? This is the first thing: this is the AirPort base station, and it looks like this, right like that, and so the AirPort base station is really cool…

 And, of course, industrial design:

 So what about the computer side of things? Well, iBook is the first computer ever designed right from the start to be optimized for wireless communications, and so right in every iBook are two built-in antennas…Then, we have an AirPort card, a small little card, and the iBook is designed to accept it. So let’s take a look at that. As you know, Apple pioneered this way of adding memory without taking your whole portable apart through simply lifting the keyboard. Well, we have enhanced that now to take an AirPort card, and as you see, there’s a space right there in every iBook ready for an AirPort card, and you can drop one in, just like that, and connect the cable that comes from the antenna. Right? You saw that? I’ll go back. Just connect that cable and push it in, and now your iBook is AirPort functioning. You are on the wireless network. All the software detects the AirPort card and automatically sets it up for wireless networking without going through hours of configuring your computer. It all happens automatically. This has been a major effort on the part of Apple’s hardware and software engineers and also Lucent.

 This paragraph is a bit extraneous, other than the fact it is personally meaningful: my first Apple computer was an iMac G4, the following all-white generation, with the same AirPort card installation. I remember being amazed at just how easy it was to add wireless . And now, here I am, 22 years later, still using an Apple laptop to write this Article.

 Apple HomeView

 Two weeks ago I wondered how long I was for the Apple ecosystem ; one product I was definitely not interested in was the then-forthcoming Apple smarthome product:

 What struck me about Gurman’s article is just how unenthused I am by an Apple smarthome product. Some of this is fatigue from a decade of Siri disappointment and skepticism about the company’s ability to deliver on a voice-centric product. More than that, however, I bristle at the idea of introducing Apple’s constraints to more parts of my life.

 Those constraints aren’t just about things like full disk access. To the extent that Apple delivers on integration with things like thermostats and door locks is the extent to which they work with 3rd-party device makers; the problem is that third party device makers mostly suck, particularly from a software perspective. Even if Siri were perfect, Apple will have the challenge of delivering an experience that isn’t defined by the lowest common denominator.

 What I’m much more interested in is controlling the software layer myself. The fact of the matter is that with AI you can decompile almost all existing software — there is a revolution happening in gaming over the past few weeks, as game after game is decompiled to source and ported to any platform you wish — and you can write your own. That means my software that interacts with my agent in the way I want it to for everything; that’s way more exciting than praying Apple delivers the right API and that 3rd-party developers don’t suck.

 That product is called Apple HomeView , and some prominent Apple observers don’t get the point. John Gruber wrote on Daring Fireball :

 My skepticism boils down to the question of why anyone would want to add one (or more!) additional ever-present screens to our homes and lives. Phones can stay in our pockets until we need them. Watches remain on our wrists. HomePods can be tucked away unobtrusively in corners, and remain fully useful. HomeView needs to be in a prominent location for its display to serve any practical purpose. Apple’s initial pitch for it doesn’t earn that prominence for me.

 I understand Gruber’s skepticism, particularly given the product’s truly atrocious introductory video . Beyond the overall stress-inducing nature of the suburban family scene depicted, most of the use cases, as Gruber notes, are nonsensical: to take a particularly egregious example, why would the teenage daughter look at a message from her clandestine boyfriend on the HomeView instead of her iPhone (which has to be present on the network and unlocked in the past several hours for that functionality to even work)? Apple was, in this particular case, trying to show off HomeView’s multi-user capability, which is based on facial recognition, but my biggest takeaway is that maybe highly produced marketing videos sold as product keynotes aren’t the worst idea in the world.

 In fact, I think that HomeView is pretty compelling. Smarthome functionality is genuinely useful:

 Years ago I set up a small monitor on the side of our condo’s living room for the kids to play video games; I happened to have a Raspberry Pi on hand, which I used to set up a service called DAKboard . DAKboard showed the time, the weather, the family calendar, and a rotating collection of photos. It has, in the intervening years, been one of our most-used and most-beloved pieces of technology, looked at multiple times a day every day.

 Thermostats are finicky and hard to use; it’s much better to be able to program them from your phone, or from a touch device. The problem for me in my current home is that my thermostats seem to mysteriously lose their connection to my home automation system every few weeks.

 Doorbells are critical in a world of e-commerce, especially when it comes to the dreaded “signature required”; incorporating them with your devices, along with a screen to see who is at the door, is a no-brainer. Unfortunately for me my doorbells also seem to get randomly disconnected, and I never notice until I miss a delivery.

 Cameras are a useful security measure, but only if you can actually view them. The issue is — you guessed it — that they often become inaccessible or are non-intuitive to use, particularly the moment you need them.

 Sometimes I want to access information without using my hands, like when I am cooking. You can prop up an iPhone or iPad in the kitchen, but what do you do when it goes to sleep in the middle of a recipe?

 I have, of course, just laid out five compelling use cases for the HomeView, but it wasn’t hard! These are all real, genuinely useful capabilities for a new home device. And notice what the limiting factor is for the middle three: actually getting different devices to work together reliably.

 Apple’s Trust Dividend

 That’s why the other exciting part about Apple’s HomeView announcement actually hearkened back to the original AirPort: Apple Home Collection. From Apple’s press release :

 Apple today announced Apple Home Collection, a new lineup of smart home accessories — including indoor and outdoor cameras, thermostats, temperature sensors, and a video doorbell and door lock — designed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. These new accessories are simple to set up starting with one tap with iPhone, and everything is managed through the Apple Home app — no separate app or account required. Each accessory is encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home, so only users and the people they choose can access their home data.

 Building on the thousands of Works with Apple Home and Matter accessories available today, Apple Home Collection offers customers a new array of recommended products to better understand what’s happening inside and outside their home, manage access, and keep the temperature just right throughout the day. Availability for all products begins in December, with select accessories available starting early 2027.

 “Apple Home Collection makes it easy to choose smart home accessories with confidence,” said Matthew Costello, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “Working closely with industry leaders LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, we designed every accessory to work seamlessly with Apple Home, so managing your home is simple, reliable, and private.”

 Apple doesn’t have to do everything itself in the home, just as they didn’t have to invent wireless networking in 1999; what they need to do is “marry [partner’s] technology with [their] ease-of-use technology”, and I’m optimistic they’ve done exactly that with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The key detail is “no separate app or account required”; that points to deep integration with Apple products, from setup to day-to-day usage.

 Again, I’m not sure I’m the target customer for this (although the automatically unlocking door locks look awesome); my solution to incompatible or flakey integrations is to use AI to build my own customized software. I’m under no illusions, however, that I am a normal consumer who wants the benefits of technology without the headaches; I trust Apple, more than anyone else, to at least aspire to delivering on that vision, and these 2nd-party partnerships are a great start.

 The second part where you may trust Apple more than any other company is with privacy. Jobs was talking about privacy as a selling point 27 years ago, and Apple has only doubled down since then. In the case of HomeView specifically there is that facial recognition feature, tied to your own hardware; more broadly, if there is any company you might entrust with tracking your more private spaces it is Apple, both because of promises they make with their technology and also their consistent stance on not using customer data. Indeed, Apple’s privacy umbrella is strong enough that LG’s very sketchy privacy track record is likely to be a non-issue amongst potential customers.

 Apple’s Trust Deficit

 From Bloomberg, in 2016 :

 Apple Inc. has disbanded its division that develops wireless routers, another move to try to sharpen the company’s focus on consumer products that generate the bulk of its revenue, according to people familiar with the matter. Apple began shutting down the wireless router team over the past year, dispersing engineers to other product development groups, including the one handling the Apple TV, said the people, who asked not to be named because the decision h...

blogs.content:
Release: llm-echo 0.5

 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account.

 Example usage:

 uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage

 Outputs:

 First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say.
{
 "prompt": "hi there",
 "system": "",
 "attachments": [],
 "stream": true,
 "previous": []
}
Token usage: 2 input, 24 output

 Tags: llm

We all consider Anthropic an AI company.

 But what if it’s a cloud?

 Anthropic is growing much faster than the other clouds : 15x last year. GCP’s growth is far behind at 82%. But at current growth rates, Anthropic is closer to GCP’s pace, doubling next year. 1

 In revenue terms, Anthropic is about 30% the size of AWS & Azure & nearly half the size of GCP.

 Anthropic is the fastest growing but the smallest of the four. At current growth rates, it would pass Azure in about three years & AWS in about three & a half. 4 Only GCP, now growing slightly faster than Anthropic’s current pace, would stay ahead. But Anthropic has the most concentrated business : 2 customers accounted for nearly 25% of revenue in 2025. 5

 Each started with a wedge to earn the cloud moniker : Amazon with ecommerce ; Google with search & ads ; Microsoft with the operating system. Anthropic’s angle : many of the best AI models in the world & the leading coding harness, Claude Code. 87% of businesses on Ramp that buy a coding agent buy Claude Code, up 56 points in a year. 6

 Anthropic exerts its pricing power in this market, charging more per task than others : Claude Opus 5.5 costs $5.98 per task on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, against $3.26 for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra & $1.99 for Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. 7

 It has the narrowest product offering, but it has made a record-breaking start with AI models, artifacts & design.

 Growth needs capacity, & Anthropic has planned for it. It has made the largest data center commitments of the four : $518b, nearly 8x its $67b Q3 run rate, while AWS, Microsoft & Google have committed about 1x to 2x theirs. 3

 Each of these businesses is building its own chips, scaling data centers with debt, developing &/or reselling models, & managing infrastructure to support AI.

 If it rains like a cloud & computes like a cloud… That’s how we should evaluate Anthropic.

 Using Wall Street’s estimates, a standalone GCP would be worth roughly $1t to $2.3t. 8 At $1.5t to $2t, Anthropic would be valued equally to GCP, on two-thirds the revenue & far faster growth over the past year. 9

---

 Anthropic’s annualized revenue rose from $65b at the end of July to about $71.5b at the end of September, 10% in two months or about 4.9% a month. Compounded over twelve months, 1.049^12 ≈ 1.77, a run rate near $127b by September 2027. The September figure is an estimate with a range of $69b to $74b; across that range the next twelve months imply 1.4x to 2.2x. Quarterly revenue grew faster, 45% from Q2 to Q3, but most of that gain came early in the quarter, so the exit pace is the better guide. Sources : CNBC, August 17, 2026 ; Syz Group, October 15, 2026 .  ↩︎

 For AWS, Microsoft & Google, leases signed but not yet started, primarily for data centers, as of June 30, 2026, company-wide rather than for the cloud segment alone : Amazon $137.2b ( 10-Q ), Microsoft $329.1b starting fiscal 2027 through 2033 ( 10-K ), Alphabet $85.2b starting 2026 through 2031 ( 10-Q ).
